utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the purpose of the hearing today and tomorrow is to determine the appropriate sentence for the accused, Mr. Milan Babic. On the 27th of January, 2004, the accused pled guilty to the crime of persecutions, a crime against humanity, for his role in crimes committed against Croats and other non-Serbs by Serb forces in Croatia during 1991. Specifically, the accused admitted that he was a co-perpetrator in a joint criminal enterprise whose goal was the forceful removal of the non-Serb population from the territory of the so-called Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, otherwise known as the SAO Krajina. Other participants in this joint criminal enterprise included Slobodan Milosevic, Milan Martic, Goran Hadzic, Jovica Stanisic, Franko Simatovic, Vojislav Seselj, and Generals Blagoje Adzic and Ratko Mladic, nearly all of whom have either been charged by this Tribunal or are currently detained at this Tribunal or are in trial. The purpose of the joint criminal enterprise was accomplished in part through the crime of persecutions to which this accused has pled guilty. It is important to note that the -- encompassed within this single crime of persecutions are the crimes of extermination and murder, detentions and inhumane treatment, deportation, and the destruction of private, cultural, and religious property. Accordingly, the charge of persecutions attempts in a single umbrella charge to capture the full range and severity of the crimes committed by the members of the joint criminal enterprise, including this accused, against Croat and other non-Serb civilians. The law of the Tribunal sets forth four factors that the Trial Chamber must consider in sentencing. One, the gravity of the offence; two, the individual circumstances of the convicted person; three, any mitigating or aggravating circumstances; and four, the sentencing practices of the former Yugoslavia. In this case, however, I think it's helpful to think of two competing factors that the Trial Chamber will have to consider in reaching a sentence for this accused. On the one hand, the Trial Chamber will have to consider the gravity of the offence and this accused's role in that offence. On the other hand, the Court will have to consider and weigh the accused's plea of guilty, his acceptance of responsibility, and his cooperation with this Tribunal and the Prosecution. With respect to the first part of the equation, the Prosecution submits that it is the law of the Tribunal that the gravity of the offence must weigh very, very heavily. In fact, the Prosecution submits that it is the single most important factor that must be considered by the Court at sentencing. The accused has pled guilty to one of the most serious crimes known to mankind, and the suffering, the pain, and the loss caused by these crimes are immense. More than 230 Croats and other non-Serbs were murdered, and thousands of others were subjected to discriminatory measures, detained in inhumane conditions, driven from their homes, or had their personal, religious, or cultural property destroyed. The destruction from these crimes is still felt acutely to this day and will be continued to be felt for years and years to come. On the issue of the gravity of the crimes, the Prosecution during this hearing will offer into evidence both written and oral evidence. With respect to the written evidence, the Prosecution will offer as exhibits the statements of five victims who give evidence about the crimes committed and how they affected -- how these crimes affected them and their families. These statements have already been provided to the Court as attachments to our sentencing brief and have been provided to the Defence. I will briefly described what is stated in these statements, but before I do, I would like to situate the crimes at issue on a map that we will also tender into evidence. I will ask the case manager to put the map on the ELMO. This was a map provided to the Prosecution by this accused. It is a map from the Republika Srpska from 1993. However, it is possible to see on this map the SAO Krajina where the crimes occurred in 1991. It's hard -- this map is so big it's hard to capture. If the case manager could show the portion that's marked A, which is just moving it a little bit over and get the -- there we go. And then maybe if we -- is it possible to back out to get -- to get more -- okay. The area on the map that is marked as A, and if the case manager could just point to the -- that area, that -- there -- that area that's marked A with that boundary is the area which was the SAO Krajina in 1991. With this map is also a translation of the text that is on the map, but for the present purposes, it's the map itself which is useful. So the area that is marked A is the SAO Krajina from 1991. The area which is next to that marked B is Western Slavonia, and the area that is marked C is Eastern Slavonia. The areas B and C are not at issue in this case. It is area A which is at issue and the area that is was the SAO Krajina and the area of which this accused was the president during the crimes in question. Now, I would like to indicate on this map in the area A where the crimes were committed. If the case manager could point to the villages there in the north-eastern part of the SAO Krajina are the villages of Bacin, Dubica, and Cerovljani which are referenced in paragraph 15A (i) of the indictment the first group of crimes committed in those villages. In the middle of the SAO Krajina are the villages of Saborsko - the case manager's pointing to them now - Saborsko, Poljanak, and Lipovaca which are referenced in paragraph 15(a)(ii) of the indictment. And finally just to the west of Knin -- you have to push the map up a little bit there. In the southern part of the region of the SAO Krajina are the villages just to the west of Knin are the villages of Skabrnja and Nadin and Bruska, and these villages are the site of crimes which are described in paragraphs 15(a)(iii) and (iv) of the indictment. And then Knin is there evident on the map and the relationship to these villages. Thank you. Now if I could briefly describe to Your Honours the content of the five victims' statements which will be tendered into evidence by the Prosecution. One witness from Dubica describes how many Croats fled this village, the village of Dubica, during the conflict, and that on the 20th of October, 1991, 53 civilians who remained including many elderly and women were rounded up by the Krajina militia and taken to the local fire station where they were guarded by local Serbs and the JNA. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness himself was released, but he later learned that remaining detainees, along with other detainees from the surrounding villages, were massacred and buried in a mass grave, and in fact, many of these victims were later found in a mass grave after the war. When the witness returned to his village in 1995, he discovered that 13 houses, including his own, and the Catholic church in his village were levelled to the ground. A second witness provides evidence about the attack by Serb forces on Skabrnja on the 18th November 1991. This witness tells how Serb soldiers including JNA soldiers and SAO Krajina soldiers intentionally, deliberately executed civilians during the attack, including elderly and women. A third witness describes how the Krajina militia came to her village of Bruska on the 21st of December, 1991, and massacred ten civilians, nine Croats, and one Serb who happened to be visiting with the Croats and was himself also killed, and also seriously injured the witness herself. When the witness returned to her village after the war, she found her house looted. Another witness provides evidence about attacks on the village of Poljanak and how civilians were literally lined up and executed. Finally, a witness provides evidence about his arrest by Martic's militia and his detention in the old hospital in Knin. The witness was detained with approximately 120 other Croats and provides evidence in his statement about the severe mistreatment and abuse that occurred at that prison. I have just briefly described what these witnesses say, but the full details of the horrors that they experienced are -- have been -- will be provided into evidence for the consideration of the Trial Chamber. In addition, the Prosecution will offer into evidence as an exhibit the report of Colonel Ivan Grujic, the head of the Croatian office for detainees and missing persons, which provides comprehensive data about civilians who were killed, who went missing during the war, and about those who were detain. This data and report and information, including detailed information about exhumations, will provide the Court with a basis to assess the scale of the crimes to which this accused has pled guilty. Finally, the Prosecution and the Defence as a joint witness will call Dr. Mladen Loncar, who as I've said will be led by Ms. Sabine Bauer. Mr. Loncar is a psychiatrist with expertise in dealing with victims of war or war crimes and he will testify about the effects on the victims of the crimes in Croatia that occurred in this case. In conjunction with this testimony, the Prosecution will offer into evidence the report and the CV of Mr. Loncar. In addition to the gravity of the offence, the Trial Chamber will have to consider that the accused's role in these crimes was significant. It is accepted that the accused was not the architect of the plan and was far from being the most important actor in the joint criminal enterprise. However, during the times of the crimes, the accused as president of the so-called SAO Krajina held the highest political office in the region. Starting in August of 1991, this accused knew that other members of the joint criminal enterprise were forcibly resettling the Croat and other non-Serb population from the targeted areas, and he was conscious that the crimes of mistreatment and prisons, deportations, forcible transfers, and destruction of property were being committed. He also knew that killings were a likely outcome of the pursuit of the joint criminal enterprise. Yet this accused retained his office during this time, participated in the arming of the Serbs and in the creation of the staffing of political and military structures for a Serb entity in Croatia and in obtaining financing for these military structures. At no time did the accused have control over the military or Krajina police force that committed the crimes however. In addition the Trial Chamber will have to consider the conduct of the accused since the crimes in question, and on this issue the Prosecution will offer into evidence the testimony of Ambassador Peter Galbraith, who was the American ambassador to Croatia from 1993 to 1998, from the Milosevic case. So first and foremost, the Trial Chamber will have to consider the gravity of the offence and the accused's role in the crimes. On the other side of the equation, however, it must be recognised that this accused initiated contact with the Prosecution before he was charged, cooperated extensively with the Prosecution, testified in the case against Slobodan Milosevic, has agreed to testify in other cases before this Tribunal, and has pled guilty and accepted responsibility for the charges that were brought against him. Some might say that a man who has committed a crime against humanity should at a minimum take these steps and that he should get no credit for these actions. However, in fact, it is the rare accused who does so, and the beneficiaries of the accused's guilty plea and cooperation are this Tribunal, the process of the search for truth, the citizens of the former Yugoslavia, the goal of reconciliation, and most importantly perhaps, the victims of the crimes themselves. The accused's guilty plea and testimony send the message that these crimes did happen. It is not just the Tribunal that says so. It is not just the Prosecution that says so. But one of the persons responsible for the crimes says so. This does not erase the crimes that were committed. It does not excuse them. But, rather, it acknowledges and affirms them on behalf of the victims. In this regard, it serves as an important step in the process of reconciliation which is one of the critical goals of this institution. Mr. Mladen Loncar will testify not only about the effects of the crimes on the victims but also about the positive effects from the accused's guilty plea and his acknowledgement of responsibility. In addition, the Prosecution will offer into evidence a selection of quotations from the accused, from his testimony and his interviews with the Prosecution, which speak to his responsibility for the crimes in question. Further, the accused's cooperation and testimony are a significant step towards establishing the truth and towards bringing those responsible for these crimes to account for their actions. As an indicator of the significance of the accused's testimony of, the Prosecution will tender into evidence a list of documents provided and authenticated by Mr. Babic during his testimony. Those persons responsible for the crimes in which the accused participated, and here we are referring in particular to those at the very top, those with the most responsibility, often planned the crimes and executed them with great secrecy, taking care to hide their actions and ensuring that there would be few records of their misdeeds. Further, they took significant steps to cover up their crimes and mislead the international community while they were happening and after they occurred. It is an uncomfortable reality in the search for truth that only by hearing the testimony of those who were on the inside, those who played a role in the crimes themselves that the full truth of what happened and who was responsible will be known. For these reasons, the steps that the accused has taken should be encouraged by this Court. Others in his position should be encouraged and should get the message that it is important and valuable and worthwhile to step forward, take responsibility, and tell the truth. Once the Trial Chamber has heard all the evidence and arguments at this sentencing hearing, it will need to weigh within the framework of the law and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal these two competing considerations, on the one hand the gravity of the offence and the accused's role in that offence; and on the other hand, the accused's plea of guilty and his cooperation. At the end of the hearing on the evidence, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff will address the Court and make arguments as to the appropriate sentence on behalf of the Prosecution. At this time, I would like with the Court's permission to tender into evidence the exhibits that I've referenced on behalf of the Prosecution. The first exhibit, and I believe they will be marked P -- PS -- PS1, is a statement of five -- of the five victims, crime based witnesses, victim impact statements. These statements have been redacted where appropriate to protect the identity of certain of the victims. Exhibit PS2 is the map of the region I showed during the opening statement which has been marked with different sections. PS3 is the report of Colonel Ivan Grujic head of the Croatian Office for Detainees and Missing Persons. The report is entitled "Missing people, displaced people, and killed people in the Republic of Croatia during the war years 1990 to 1992." Exhibit PS4 is a selection of quotations from the accused, from his testimony and interviews with the Prosecution. Exhibit PS5 is the testimony of Ambassador Peter Galbraith, the US ambassador to Croatia from 1993 to 1998, from the Milosevic case. Exhibit PS6 is the list of documents either provided by Mr. Babic or authenticated by Mr. Babic during his testimony in the Milosevic case. And finally, Your Honours, Exhibit PS7 is the complete transcript of Mr. Babic's testimony from the Milosevic case and his interviews with the Prosecution. These are voluminous and the Prosecution hesitated about whether to provide it to the Trial Chamber. However, it was finally decided that because there may be references to various passages contained within those, testimony or interviews, that it would be prudent for the Trial Chamber to have those into evidence. So those are being provided as well as PS -- Exhibit PS7. As mentioned before these are all being tendered pursuant to Rules 89(F), 92 bis, and with the agreement of the Defence that they can be put into evidence and considered by the Trial Chamber. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. From what I heard from Mr. Whiting, I take it that there are no objections to admission into evidence of the exhibits then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just checking, Mr. Whiting. I noticed that in the material that had been provided to the Chamber prior to the sentencing hearing there was some -- there are some differences in numbering. Sometimes the B/C/S version has numbered paragraphs whereas the translation into English has not, which of course doesn't make it very easy to make references to specific parts of -- of those statements if we need to refer to them in our judgement. I'm not going to invite you to -- to submit them again because that would be the third time and a lot of loss of paper, but the Chamber will consider how to resolve this problem. But in general terms it's not only in this case that this happens, if numbering -- paragraph numbering is added in a document, it's preferred by the Chamber that's it's done in all languages and not just in one or two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for the inconvenience. We will look this afternoon to see whether there is a way to solve that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the possibilities would be that since we have not taken any decision yet, that you would number them before we finally decide to admit them into evidence, at least one copy, and then of course in our personal copies it could be added at a later stage, but that might be one of the solutions. Then, Mr. Whiting, the -- I would like to address the Defence. Would you like to make a few opening remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then please do so, Mr. Fogelnest. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: May it please the Trial Chamber, I think that during the course of this hearing you will find very little if any conflict between the positions of the Defence and the Prosecution with one exception that I'll mention in a moment. Consistent with the intention expressed by Mr. Babic from the time he came forward over two years ago to volunteer to come before the Tribunal, we on the Defence and the Prosecution's side have worked together to try to bring the truth before this Trial Chamber and this Tribunal and for the purposes of history, and rather than acting as adversaries, there has been a remarkable degree of cooperation. The only point where we may differ is a legal issue as lawyers sometimes do with respect to the application of perhaps an aggravating circumstance in connection with Mr. Babic's role as a civil/political leader, and that is more of a legal argument rather than a factual one. The goal of all parties, Mr. Babic, the members of the Prosecution team, and the members of the Defence team has been to bring the truth forward. All of us, our client included, believe that the way to make a better world is to have the truth about what occurred at this period of time in this part of the world be understood by the world so that we can then go forward and understand what happened and perhaps find ways from that understanding to prevent it from happening again. We view our role as assisting this Tribunal in making those determinations. We have provided a great deal of information before this hearing. Prosecution has done a wonderful job in assisting and gathering that information, much of it provided by Mr. Babic. We will present few witnesses. There is no disagreement. We have had an opportunity to speak with Mr. Loncar and endorse what he has to say. They have had an opportunity to meet with our witness, and I believe they will have no quarrel with anything he says. Again, and I can't underscore this enough, it is the goal of all of us to help you determine what the truth is and help you weigh and assess the appropriate factors so that you can come to a just and fair verdict and sentence that will serve the goals of this Tribunal and ultimately the community of the world and perhaps in some small way putting a stop to the kinds of things that happened. These crimes are occurring, as we speak, in other parts of the world. The work done by this Tribunal is the beginning of what we hope to be a better civilisation as human beings evolve and learn from what has occurred in the past and look for solutions so that it doesn't occur in the future. Mr. Babic has come forward to attempt to help in this process. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. You will have to weigh the contribution he makes, the contribution he has made, the courage it has taken for him to do that, which is not in dispute, against the gravity of the crime, which cannot be overstated. What has happened in the Balkans is horrendous. You will have to assess his role and weigh that against the other factors and then do a calculation to translate that into what you feel is an appropriate sentence. We will assist you as best we can, and we thank you for the opportunity of doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fogelnest. Ms. Bauer, addressing you, how much time would you think the examination of Mr. Loncar will take?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I estimate at the moment between one and a half, maximum two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Maximum two hours. Let's then start with the witness, and may I ask you one thing, you consider him an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: He has provided an expert report which we in due course ask the Court to tender into evidence. And as far as we know, the Defence does not object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm asking it because -- because of the solemn declaration I'll ask him to give to the Court, and that would be then the solemn declaration of an expert rather than of a witness. He will not testify on the specific facts relating to the case but rather on his experience as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see Mr. Usher has already left the courtroom, so I take it that the expert witness will enter the courtroom soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning. I take it that you're Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On request of both parties, you have been called to provide the Court with the expertise you have, your professional expertise, and before doing so, I'd like you to make a solemn declaration as an expert. Since we haven't got them in writing in B/C/S, I'll read it part by part. Will you please repeat it. I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That I will do so faithfully, independently, impartially, and with full respect for the duty of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loncar, please be seated. You will be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bauer. Questioned by Ms. Bauer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: My name is Mladen Loncar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, you are a psychiatrist in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you specialised in traumatology?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you assist victims of war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to this extent, you managed two major national programmes in Croatia, and I would like you to shortly describe to the Court which these two programmes are.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I was the head of the Medical Centre for Human Rights from 1992. I have worked on international programmes of socio- and psychological help to victims of war which were sponsored by international organisations such as the European Union, the World Health Organisation, some governments of Western European countries, and the second project I worked on is a national program of psychosocial and medical assistance to victims of war in Croatia. I have been in co-ordination with four regional centres. The centres are called the Regional Centres for Psychological Trauma in Zagreb, Osijek, Split, and Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loncar, the Office of the Prosecutor has asked you to prepare as report, an expert report which deals in principle with two main areas, one is the impact of wartime traumas on the physical and mental well-being of four different witness group, many of which -- all of which were part of this indictment; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And secondly, in this report you concentrated on the effect of Mr. Babic's guilty plea on the victims' group as well as the perpetrator group, including its contribution to reconciliation. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I'd like that -- I would like to offer the expert report, including the curriculum vitae, of Dr. Loncar to be marked as Prosecution sentencing Exhibit number 8. As a small information which -- we have renumbered the B/C/S version in order to correspond to the English version in terms of pagination so Dr. Loncar and Mr. Babic can follow better the B/C/S version of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loncar, before we talk about the main conclusions of your report, I'd like shortly to digress and read you your educational background, and if you concur with me if you can just confirm at the end. In 1987, you received a graduate degree in medicine in Novi Sad. You commenced subsequently a residence in neuropsychiatry which you had to interrupt due to the war operations. You restarted that residence and graduated in Zagreb in 1998. In 1999, you completed a post-graduate study of social psychiatry at the medical school in Zagreb, which at the same time qualified you as a court-appointed expert in this field. In 2003, you completed another master's degree in social psychiatry at the medical school in Zagreb. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, could you for the benefit of the court please shortly explain what social psychiatry is.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Social psychiatry is a branch of psychiatry which deals with the relationship between a community and a patient with a mental disorder and the effect that a mental disorder has on a social community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this context, Dr. Loncar, you participated in numerous conferences, and you also have a huge list of publications on this issue which Your Honours can see from the attached curriculum vitae which is attached to the report. Now, Dr. Loncar, could you explain the Court, please, what was your personal experience during the war in 1991 which led you to focus your work on treating victims of trauma which occurred during the war or after war.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I must say to the Chamber that I spent two months in a camp in Begejci and Vojvodina in Serbia, and this was my personal motive. When I saw what was happening to other of my inmates, there were some 5 or 600 of us, I decided to spend some professional time in work with war victims. As a professional, as a doctor, as an humanitarian, I wanted to invest my knowledge to help primarily victims, and within my work also I wanted to work on the prevention of violations of human rights, because this is an integral part of looking after human health.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of this experience, Doctor, did you found the medical centre in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. During the exchange that was mediated by the Red Cross, I arrived in Zagreb. At the beginning of 1992, I gathered a team of doctors who had empathy for psychological trauma. We established the Medical Centre for the -- for Human Rights. The main goal of that centre was to help victims of psycho-trauma. And when we analysed what we did, we decided to present the results of our work both to foreign experts as well as to the organisations that may have had some influence on the events in the former Yugoslavia. I primarily refer to the World Health Organisation and the organisation for protection of human rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on page 1 of your report, Dr. Loncar, you did outline actually the different projects you were working on as a result; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, how many victims did the centre as a whole deal with since 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Since that day until today, approximately 5.000 victims were treated and went through our centre for human rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were this only victims of Croatia or did this extend beyond Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: These were mostly victims from Croatia, refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. We have worked in Bosnia and Herzegovina too. And following that, we started also working with the victims from Kosovo and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the employees of the centre that you employ, are they multi-ethnic or ever a single ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: From 1992 until today, over 30 persons went through the centre of different ethnic backgrounds including Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 223 of your report, Doctor, you outline the method of the medical centre in assembling information through taking statements of victims. Would you please tell the Court what the major value is of taking such statements?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The method of taking statements is a kind of therapy which started being used in the 1970s, in the last century. It was also used in Chile during the military regime and it also proved to be useful in the area affected by earthquake. The method is as follows: The victim together with its counsellor puts in writing his or her experience and then works over it with the counsellor. This is a document that has as a symbolic value but also a legal one. So the primary therapeutic effect of this method is that the victim while giving a statement goes from being a victim to being a witness; therefore, changes his or her status. And this acknowledges society-wise the experience of this victim and gives it a value in society as is such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Doctor, what other more secondary purposes do those statements serve?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: As a result, after the statement was given, certain analyses and studies were done, and the information collected in this manner was presented to the public. When I say "to the public," I mean organisations dealing with protection of human rights which could have certain impact in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and could have had certain impact on bringing the war to an end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, in your report you presented several factual conclusions, and if we could please look at page 3, the penultimate paragraph. Could you please tell the Court how you arrived at the number of detainees?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The number of detainees in the Knin camps was arrived at after working and taking statements from the victims. This figure pertains to the period between 1991 and 1995, and this figure approximately coincides with the figure given by the official commission for the same period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 9, if would you kindly look, you arrive at factual conclusions as to the municipality Hrvatska Dubica, which was a part of this indictment, in terms of destruction. How -- how did -- what was the source of these figures?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The information listed on page 9 is the information that I collected after having visited the area and after having had contacts with the victims and returnees. This is how I gathered and collected the information on destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have contact with the victims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I had contacts with the victims before, and as for this data here, this is a result of contacts which began early this year and lasted until a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 11, subsequent pages, you described people who witnessed the killings of relatives. What was the source of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The source of this information and these statements is our work with the displaced persons. After their family members were killed, the families were displaced. They became refugee. We visited refugee centres. We talked too people about the events in their regions, and then after having taken statements, we arrived at these details, this information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, could you please return to the first victim group, and that's on page 3, the victims of incarceration. On page 4, you list all the forms of mistreatment -- 3 and 4, all the forms of mistreatment detainees suffered and divided it mainly by mental and physical abuse. Could you please just very briefly list some of the mental abuse you learned about after talking to former detainees.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, and I will mention them individually. The most frequent psychological abuse in prisons and camps ranged from confinement in dark, cramped areas, in cells, and also exposing victims to extreme light, deprivation of sleep, frequent awakenings during night, not allowing prisoners to rest, forcing them to sing songs which were humiliating for victims, threats or taking them to fake executions, forcing them to watch or listen the beatings and torture of other prisoners. And these were the most frequent forms of psychological torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what is the result in terms of mental disorders or effects this can have on former detainees?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Mental disorders, which are found in former detainees, are three disorders. One is the post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety disorder, and affective disorders or disorders of the mood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you shortly, please, explain what a post-traumatic stress disorder is and which symptoms this disorder exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder has several features. The first one or criterion A in order to develop a post-traumatic stress disorder is an experience which is outside of normal human experiences, which means that a patient was exposed to threats or came close to being killed and was exposed to a deadly fear. As a result of that, three kinds of symptoms develop. These symptoms are linked with this traumatic experience, and the second group of symptoms are insomnia, attention Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disorder, occasional anger outbursts and so on, and the third group of symptoms are those that have to do with alienating the victim from the society or community, tendency to spend time alone and lack of will to participate in normal human activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there a development of such an acute post-traumatic stress disorder to a more severe disorder of that person?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: It is possible. Post-traumatic stress disorder normally appears within the first three to six months. This is when it starts developing usually. Some people who develop this disorder, PTSD, after at least of two years of symptoms listed within this disorder develop another disorder which is classified in the psychiatric literature, and it is called permanent personality disorder. It is listed under the code 62.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the effect of a permanent personality disorder on the person?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: What is typical for permanent personality disorder is an affective change. The patients normally describe this change as feeling different than they used to feel before. So this is a kind of an emotional bluntness. The patient is unable to experience any pleasure, and they become indifferent to life in general. They lose any interest in social contacts and usual day-to-day activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that leads me to the next question, what the impact is of such a disorder on the person's ability to manage everyday life and to function in society.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: What is typical for both of these disorders, PTSD and permanent personality disorder, is that the patients have a weakened ability to function socially on a day-to-day basis, which makes them lose their ability to work, and this depends on the intensity of their disorder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, is there a specific starting date for such a post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: If you mean the time period, if that's what you're referring to, then I can tell you that it develops within three to six months after the traumatic experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any time that it can develop at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The medical literature and also practice are aware of where this develops after several years. This is a so-called delayed PTSD, and the symptoms that I have described appear several years after the traumatic experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would trigger this delayed start?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: That could be either a banal, repeated trauma or a decompensation due to new life experiences which can remind the victim of the original traumatic experience. Usually we call this secondary traumatisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, how many camp detainees did you have did talk suffered from such a post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: In the research done by our medical centre, we found that approximately 80 per cent of former detainees suffers from PTSD, obviously in various intensity, from mild ones to grave cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there any recovery from post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: When this comes to recovery, let us go back to criterion A, which is the traumatic experience that the patient suffered. This cannot be erased. This is recorded permanently in the patient's memory, all of these traumatic events and experiences. However we can treat symptoms or consequences of this psycho-trauma. Our experience has shown that a patient can be brought to a remission stage where he can function socially both within the community as a whole and within his or her family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my concluding question before possibly the break is: You listed in the beginning to other disorders that frequently occur in former camp detainees which is the anxiety and an affective disorder. Could you just shortly explain what an affective disorder is?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Affective disorders or disorders of the mood is a disorder which frequently comes as a result of a psychological trauma, and it can range from a mild depression to a severe one. What is typical for this disorder is a loss of ability to experience pleasure, a permanent fatigue, also bad mood, which is experienced by the patient's lack of interest in day-to-day activities, difficulty in concentrating, difficulty in focussing, and it is usually accompanied by depressive emotions, and by this I am referring to outbursts of crying and sorrow. Patients who experience extreme symptoms can also develop certain morbid features and suicidal ideas. Such patients usually see no solution for their situation, and these kinds of people have a higher suicide rate when compared to people who have not experienced any traumatic events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bower, I wouldn't mind if you would continue until 10.30 and then have the break then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, in your report on pages 3 and 4, you also list the most frequent physical, long-term effects of abuse both physically and mentally, as well as -- and the prolonged detention on detainees, and you divided it in so-called direct and indirect consequences, physical consequences. Could you just briefly address the direct and indirect consequences?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Whether it comes to physical torture that the inmates have been through we are talking about the direct consequences, the direct physical consequences which are injuries that they sustain most often by blunt objects such as a baseball bat, a rifle butt, a boot and so on and so forth. This leads to the injuries to the soft tissues. At the beginning these about haematomas all over the inmates' bodies. And when it comes to the motoric system, that's bones and muscles, there were frequent injuries of the head and rib fractures due to beatings. When it comes to indirect consequences of physical abuse, we are talking about the conditions of life in such spaces where inmates were exposed to starvation, and as a result of that, we saw a sudden loss of weight and weakened immunity system. Very often we saw infectious diseases among the inmates and various other diseases of that sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your research, could you see an effect of such abuse on the mortality rate of former camp detainees?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: According to the -- our data, the risk group both for the mobility bit as well as the mortality suffered from more frequent disease than the general population. On the other hand, we have also noticed that the mortality rate among that group is higher than in the general population which was not exposed to any traumatic experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting at page 6 of your report, Doctor, you deal with a second victims' group, namely the victims of displacement and deportation. Doctor, what are the most common traumatic experiences that displaced people suffer which connects them to the other two groups, namely people that are missing a relative or a close person as well as people that have witnessed or learned about the killing of a close person?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: What is typical of all of these groups that we list in our report is the following: Usually these people suffered from a compounded trauma. For example, in the group of expelled, we find former detainees, people who had lost their home or a close member of their family or within their family they have a person missing. What is typical of all of these groups as I've already said, is that very often that they will suffer from PTSD, the mood disorder, and what is also typical of this group is the fact that they suffer from the so-called dislocation stress. This is one of the major stress situations that can happen to a person during their life. I'm talking about the -- the fact that they had to abandon their home and they had to lose the security that a familiar milieu offers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Doctor, what are sort of the typical types of illnesses that people developed, physical illnesses since you mentioned the mental already.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: What is typical of these cases due to intense accumulative stress situations, in this population we have seen hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, that is impairments in the functioning and work of their heart, arrythmias, and other heart conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there a specific age group which is specifically affected by the stress of dislocation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: There are two age groups which are at more risk than others. Those are children and elderly. Children, because they have not developed their adaptation capabilities and the little security that they had before they had to move, they lose by moving. And on the other hand we have the elderly who have already lost their adjustment abilities suffer more from the dislocation stress. Mostly people who were expelled from rural areas would mostly arrive at urban areas, and at the beginning they would be accommodated at collective accommodation centres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on pages 6 and 7 of your report, Doctor, you mention the stress-building factors on displaced people, and I'm just summarising the headings which would be the arrival in a strange place, living in overcrowded spaces, and a certain conclusion in a social and family environment. Would you like to point out a specific group which suffers -- is this -- is this a compound stress or is this sort of an individual stress or is this a development phase of the stress factors that you are mentioning in this report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: We're talking about a cumulative stress, a stress that has accumulated over a period of time from beginning of traumatic events. And this traumatic experience is also the refugee status. The -- how much a person is going to be able to cope with that will primarily depend on the age and the vulnerability of the person. The person at more risk than others are children and the elderly. Also, the level of stress will also depend on the pre-war stress status of each individual and also of their pre-morbidity status. That is how prone they were to illness before the stress event. Also, it will depend on the previous experience that the person had and whether they were able to cope with traumatic experience in the past and how they coped with those, and also it will depend on the expectations of other people and the frustration that these people experience. All this will lead to the final cumulative effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally before the break, you mentioned in this group a specific disorder called accommodation disorder. Could you just in one sentence describe what an accommodation disorder is? It's on page 9 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. This is a disorder which is called in the official classification the adjustment disorder. The clinical features are emotional disorder, the changed behaviour as a response to the well-known psycho-social stress. These people are not able to adapt to newly arisen situations. There is a press -- a presence of disturbed social contacts and inability to function at their workplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bauer. I think it's a proper time to have a break. We'll have a break until ten minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, before we move on to the next victim group, I have one last question in terms of the impact of the accumulated stress that displaced people experience. In your research, did you detect an increase in the mortality rate of such people as opposed to people -- population that doesn't go through such stress factors?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Based on our data and also based on the contact with doctors who used to work in the villages before the war, we can see that there definitely is an increase in mortality rate. Certain villages were looked at in order to see how many cases of death, natural death, they had yearly. This information was later compiled with information gathered from those same doctors who worked with their former patients who now became refugees. And to compare, let me give you figures. If before a village had five to ten cases of death a year, then after its residents became refugees, this figure rose up to 15 cases a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Than you, Doctor. Coming to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer, could I ask one additional question. I do understand that the mortality rate went up, but did you establish the causal relationship with either the removal or different housing circumstances after having become a refugee? I mean, what could you say about the causes of this higher mortality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our explanation for the increase in mortality rate is as follows: As we are dealing with accumulated stress to which various groups of refugees were exposed, unlike to conditions that existed before the war where there was no stress, these people, after becoming refugees, developed certain illnesses such as cardiac illnesses, diabetes, hypertension, and so on. So at an earlier stage in life, these illnesses appeared among refugees and led to a decrease in expected life, and this led to a decrease in life expectancy and at the same time is an explanation of the increase in mortality rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but this doesn't fully answer my question. I fully appreciate that the new conditions, especially stress conditions, could contribute to such developments, but there would be numerous other circumstances that had been changed as well. Let's just say housing, the heating of the houses which might cause other situations as far as food is concerned, other situations as far as employment is concerned. I mean, for refugees, a lot of circumstances do change, which I can imagine could also contribute to a higher rate of -- of diseases and even mortality. My question is: How could you establish that it were mainly those causes you concentrated on in your research rather than perhaps other causes which were, well, less in your field of expertise that could have contributed to a higher rate of diseases and mortality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, Your Honours, I would like to explain. When I mentioned cumulative stress or cumulative trauma, this is the fact that the traumatic experience among the refugees did not stop when they managed to leave the war-affected areas. Unfortunately, among these people, just likes said, the stress continued. The stress situation continued with their collective accommodation once they left their homes, and this is especially true of the elderly who were used to a certain pace of life. All of a sudden they were in cramped conditions with other people, different food served collectively. They were restricted to a certain area having been accommodated in sports Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. halls, hotels where their movement was restricted with regard to what they had before the war. These people experienced constant yearning for home, mourning for the life that they had before. All this contributed to what we believe has made this group of people a risk group, and that's why they started developing some conditions much earlier in their life. They developed such conditions which are expected to appear at a later stage in life, and that is why these people, or a certain percentage of these people died before the expected time, because they didn't have the adjustment capabilities. They were too exhausted by then time in order to adjust themselves to the new conditions of life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, on pages 10 to 14 of your report you deal with the impact of the traumatic experience of people that miss -- of people who either witnessed the killing of a relative or learned subsequently that a relative experienced a violent death. What is the most common trauma these people develop?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: What we have been able to notice in our work and which corresponds with the description found in professional medical journals is as follows: When somebody experiences a loss in their family, the mourning starts when the death is expected or the individual or the family is prepared for such an event. Since these deaths occurred before that time, and that those were the result of a trauma, we noticed among this population a specific reaction which we describe and which has already been described in professional literature as a pathological mourning. What is typical of these families whose members were killed, together with all the other things that I have already mentioned, since this group also belongs to the group that has experienced cumulative stress, there were members of families who were detainees, who were expelled, members of their family were killed, those people developed a specific disorder which we call a pathological mourning. What is typical of this disorder is the fact that it is accompanied by mood swings or sadness. The expected natural mourning and sadness as a result of a loss in family is about six months. In our population, this period is prolonged and becomes a disorder which we called a pathological mourning. The characteristics of this are as follows: There is an intense feeling of guilt that the surviving member of family did not do enough to save the killed person, and they feel somehow responsible for the death of the member of the family who was killed. These people blame themselves for not reacting in time, for not going and for not seeing the person who could have saved the dead person. All this leads to the development of this feeling of guilt for the death of a member -- of the member of family who was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result, what mental disabilities or disorders could develop as a result of this pathological grieving?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: This pathological grieving usually becomes a medical entity which we refer to as the depressive disorder with all the characteristics of depression ranging from the pre-morbidity to the development of fully blown depression which is characterised by mood swings, the loss of satisfaction in everyday activities, loss of concentration, fatigue, insomnia, the disorder of diet, loss of appetite. And it goes to very extreme situations of the development of suicidal thoughts and ideas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Doctor, in your report you already mentioned guilt. Is there a specific term for the guilt people that witness or that have survived maybe an attempted execution experience?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: If we're talking about guilt, in this case when I'm talking about the feeling of guilt, not the legal guilt but the psychological feeling of guilt which is a rationale, because the individual could not have had any impact on the outcome of this situation. However, this does develop as a disorder which accompanies the rest of the stress syndrome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Doctor, did you mention in your report on page 11 that this guilt is also referred to as survivor's guilt?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. It may appear in the survivors as well. Very often this feeling of guilt may turn into the survivor blaming themselves for surviving, wishing to be dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, is there -- could you detect a difference of the grieving process between people who had lost a person and knew that that person was killed as opposed to those relatives who only -- whose relatives weren't just missing and having no body or anything has been detected?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. This group of victims whose family member is missing shared cumulative traumatic experience but have their own typical characteristics which are the following: The person whose family member is missing, unlike the person whose family member is dead, the dead person was buried and there is a precise beginning of the grieving period. Depending on the structure of the personality, this person experienced the following phenomenon: The act of violence has ended and the grieving period has started. On the other hand, if there is a missing person in the family, the family develops very specific reactions within the process of searching for the missing person. From the very beginning, there is a belief and there is a denial that that person is indeed dead or was indeed killed. This period lasted up to the year 1995, where there were a number of families with a missing member of the family, and they could not come to terms with the fact that this person may be dead. This period ended in 1995, and then the second stage sets in. Then these families started believing that their family members were still detained in Serbia. These people developed fantasies that their family members were in war camps, that they were not allowed to contact them. This all lasted until the fall of Milosevic's regime when these illusions finally disappeared, because it was already too late and the whole area of the former Yugoslavia was accessible and to various organisation, and all of a sudden this was clear is that these persons were not there, and this gave rise to the third stage which was the acceptance of the possibility that the person may be dead. In that group, there is always an ambivalent wish and fantasy that the person may still be alive. There is a psychological battle with the reality of the fact and the reality is that this person is certainly dead. This leads to anxieties and feelings of anxiety which lead to fantasies in order to overcome the everyday activity and pondering upon the lot of their family members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on page 16 of your report, Doctor, you deal with the problem if still despite today neither the body of a victim was found nor the circumstances of the death could be credibly established. What impact does that have on that person?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: When it comes to the current time period when there is a flow of information among the Croats, among the families whose relatives have gone missing, a certain feeling of anger develops, an anger towards the other ethnic group. In this case we are talking about the Serbs. And there is a certain feeling of anger towards Serbs who they believe to be withholding information on their missing family members, and this leads to a further delay in resolution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what the consequence, in one word, is for reconciliation purposes amongst those two ethnic groups -- sorry, what is the consequences, in a few words.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: We are here dealing with frustration on one side and development of various negative emotions towards the other group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, as the second big part of your study you looked into the effects of Mr. Babic's admission of guilt and what effect that had on, first, the victim side, the Croat side. If you could kindly summarise that position.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. Following the admission of guilt of Mr. Babic, we can say that its impact on Croat victims could be described as follows: The perpetrator finally was given a first and a last name, so the guilt has been individualised, so to say. Therefore, negative emotions which are experienced towards the other ethnic group is diminished and finally can disappear altogether. The victims have received a certain satisfaction upon hearing that crimes have been committed, which is to say that their status of victims was officially acknowledged. And this is a process which has positive impact on Croatian victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loncar, do you know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you allow me to ask. Did you do some systematic study to the effect of the admission of guilt, or is it an impression based on what I would say incidental seeing patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please allow me to revert to the first part of my evidence when I said that the areas listed in my report as those which I toured personally from early 2004 until recently and where I spoke personally with the victims is something where official research has not been done, and this is true, but now we are talking about victims and the fact that majority of victims are accepting this as a positive sign, a positive movement. Based on my work with victims before, I can say that this -- that these negative feelings towards the other ethnic group, meaning Serbs, are becoming less acute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, do you recall that a proverb in Croatia that basically -- that summarises in a sentence what you just attempted to explain to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. In Croatia, we have a proverb which is frequently used, and it goes that what is admitted is half redressed, which means that this acknowledges the effect that an admission of guilt has upon victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you have also in your report addressed what impact of an admission of guilt has on the perpetrating side, and in order to establish whether you talked -- did you talk to any Croatian Serbs on the admission of guilt?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. I've talked mostly to Serbs from urban areas, but I also had contacts with Serbs who have returned to their homes. This work was done in mixed villages, mostly in Banovina area. I went to those villages. I talked to people of Serb ethnicity there. What I can say, and let me repeat once again that no official statistics was done. There was no official record-taking or research, so this is all a result of the exchanges in these interviews, but what I can say is that I have not met any Serbs who had a negative attitude towards the admission of guilt of Mr. Babic. What I also noticed among Serbs in Croatia is that there was a certain feeling of relief among them. The admission of guilt of Mr. Babic and the message that it sent was that we should focus on universal human emotions and treat it as such. This led to the fact that the Serbs do not feel a collective guilt now but, rather, this guilt has been individualised and attributed to a person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what is your view on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the result of the negation of any perpetrator that in -- in respect to the reconciliation between two ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I will give a brief introduction and describe what happens when there is a denial of crimes committed. Psychological experiences of the peoples in the former Yugoslavia is that they normally do not believe that justice will be done. This is a result of the fact that the legal system was always somehow oppressed by ideology or some other factors. Now to go back to the psychological dimension, let me say that there is a certain suspicion always present among the population, even when somebody is convicted for a crime, the population tends to believe that the courts are not independent, that they are under certain political or any other pressure. So they tend to question all of that. Now as to the admission of guilt and the area of which I'm speaking now, among a certain number of people the fact that there was an admission of guilt will lead to them losing all of their suspicions, because now the perpetrator himself has admitted and has shown remorse with respect to the acts committed by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And will this -- will this have an effect on both populations, the Croat population as well as the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I, as a doctor, am absolutely convinced that it will. There will be a positive impact, and let me try to explain. This admission was not only an admission of guilt, but Mr. Babic also now addressed himself both to Serbs and to Croats, and in showing his remorse he has sent a universal message that - and I'm now quoting his words - "What is most important in admission is to acknowledge that all of us belong to the same human race." Had it not been for that, the situation that reigned up to now where people lined up with their ethnic groups is what led to hatred, and then the hatred led to all the atrocities. And this act of Mr. Babic is something completely new. It has shed new light and it has sent a new message to peoples in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, and finally, what would you say takes a man like Mr. Babic, who some people will say was a moderate man and -- with no racial biases, who had Croat relatives and allegedly Croat friends throughout the war, become a nationalist who took part in ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I will try to explain that to the Trial Chamber through a situation which is known in psychiatry and psychology. If you want to change positions, views of a young man, then you have to do three things, and I think that all three things or methods did exist in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. The first method is to separate the people from one another, which means to separate people from their neighbours, in this case Croats. Then following the separation, there should be isolation. You should isolate people so that there is no flow of information, so that the flow of information is reduced, that there is as little communication as possible. And then the third stage or the third method is propaganda, Milosevic's propaganda which had an incredible impact, and it indoctrinated people. "You should tell the worst about people's neighbours and you should instil fear in them." And in that case if you do all those three things, this can lead to somebody completely changing their views, their attitudes, and becoming an extremist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loncar. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bauer. Are there -- is there any need to cross-examine Dr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. There are no questions from the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one more question for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Doctor, I would like to ask you the following. Could you tell us a bit more about the topic which I find very interesting. If I understood you well, you said that the fact that Mr. Babic has admitted his guilt has an effect on the Serbs who found an expression of their own guilt in that. Firstly, I would like to be sure that I understood you well, and secondly, I have a question. This individualisation of guilt, does it mean that in a certain way a scapegoat is found for all that happened, for all the crimes that took place, and that this person who has admitted his guilt in a certain way transferred this guilt and this guilt is now ascribed to just one person, the person who owns up to collective responsibility? First of all, tell me whether I have understood you well, and secondly, would it be useful at the psychological level to carry out this transfer of guilt or whether the case is just the opposite? Does this in a certain way minimise the individual psychology?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: If you will allow me, Your Honour, I will try and answer your question. Firstly, I adhere to what I have said, and I believe that the admission of guilt has had a positive effect on the Serbian population. I'll try and elaborate on this. The reason is the following: So far, the principle of action in the area was based on a nationalism which always accompanies homogenisation, and this is an obstacle for any kind of co-existence. Even if there hadn't been a war, it would have been detrimental for the Serbian people. In this part, in addition to his admission of guilt, Mr. Babic conveys a message. We should turn to the universality of the human race and the values of the civilised world. Let me try and answer your second question, Your Honour. When it comes to the individualisation of guilt, personally I'm deeply convinced that this doesn't mean finding a scapegoat and that this is not the fact that one person will be blamed and all will be forgotten. I believe that the individualisation of guilt is somewhat broader. In psychological terms, I can't offer you any other interpretation. In psychological terms, it means the separation between the perpetrator of Serbian origin. It means that behind every crime there is the name of the person who is responsible for a crime. Within that context, I said that the individualisation of guilt is very important. It is up to the Trial Chamber, to those who administer justice, to -- to do justice and that everybody should be taken to account for their individual crimes. When I'm talking about collective responsibility, I'm not talking about the collective or a group of people who committed crimes but collective as a nation, that there should be a distinction between the collective perpetrator of crime and the collective as the nation that the perpetrators of crime belong to. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you as well. The first is you are -- in your report, you are describing the use of a statement as an instrument both for therapeutic reasons and also to be used for research. Is there in literature -- has this method been validated in any publications or -- and would you give us the -- perhaps not immediately, but could you give us the articles in professional publications where the method as such is validated. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: If you will allow me, Your Honours, I would like to answer your question. This method was introduced in the 1970s, of the last century, in Chile. This method has been used in crisis situations in South America. In Croatia we have adopted this method. I was the first one to introduce it. There are scientific papers about this method. A book has been published about taking of statements as a therapeutic method. The author is Mr. Jensen from Denmark. He is a member of the World Health Organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it would be possible for you to write down the titles and then later on give them to us so we could try to have a look at them. I've got another question. This is a question, although it's related to page 9 of your report, it has a more general tendency, that is a question about how you used your sources and what exactly your sources were. If I take you to page 9 of your report, you write: "During the aggression more than 1.005 houses were destroyed by fire, explosives, and shelling in Hrvastka Dubica municipality. All the houses were looted before the devastation." I'd like to just use this as an example and to better understand what sources you used and how you used them. The number of 1.005, could you explain to us why you've taken 1.005 and, for example, why you didn't say more than 1.000, because 1.005 is very specific.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Allow me, Your Honours, to try and answer your question again. Over the past few months I've had meetings with returnees to that area, and this is the figure that I received from the returnees that I spoke to. The returnees themselves made a list. The village is now being reconstructed by the state, and for that reason they were aware of the very specific data, to the last number literally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless you are right. There were more than 1.005. What makes you believe that this list is not a complete one. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Some of them, families, have not returned and have not been put on the list for refurbishment. For that reason, there is a likelihood that the figure may be somewhat greater. Some of the families or their members were killed or are still missing, and the people have already dealt with the issue of their accommodation elsewhere in Croatia. So even if they return to that area, they would not be entitled to have their houses reconstructed by the government. That's why some of the families have not returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the number is related to lists which are relevant for financial support for refurbishing. Is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you do not know exactly who counted the 1.005, but you know that they appear on a list.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I know who counted them, the returnees, the victims who have returned to their destroyed houses have applied for refurbishment. They have applied to the government to help them refurbish their houses because they wanted to return and live in those houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now, you also write that all the houses were looted before the devastation. What's the exact source of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The source again are the victims themselves. Most of the people fled at the very beginning of the war. However, a certain number of the elderly remained in the village and could testify as to what had happened after a certain village was occupied. They are the main source for this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did they give this information in the framework of your psychiatric -- psychiatric-oriented research, or were -- was this information given to other authorities that then passed the information to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: They have been contacted by our medical centre, by our employees as survivors. Whether they gave their statements to some other institutions or bodies, I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you systematically interviewed them on the question whether the houses were looted before the devastation or that they were just devastated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Within the procedure of taking statements as a therapeutical method, they described the entire trauma. They described the sequence of events from the moments the troops entered the village up to the moment of their traumatic experience. And within these descriptions of these events they also described how houses were looted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have a final question. You told us what was needed to make someone change into a person with different views. You said you should separate them from others. You should bar information to come to that person, and if you used propaganda, that would be the way of changing someone other's mind in respect of the issues we're talking about. Are there -- is there the possibility that someone changes their mind without these influences?
