I mean, I've changed on certain subjects my view during my life where I was not separated, where information was not barred and where no propaganda was exercised on me. So would you accept that also without this, I would say external forces, someone could come to a different opinion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with you that opinions may change over time as we acquire more knowledge and more information. During the processing of this information, we correct our opinions. This is what is considered customary. In this specific case when I was talking about the three stages, I was talking about an extreme change of mindset. My description referred to the most extreme case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you investigate by whatever means whether the change of Mr. Babic in a -- well, let's say in a more nationalist person, was the consequence of this exterior force or exterior influence exercised upon him? I mean, did you -- did you just give us a general answer on what could bring about such changes, or do you have any knowledge specifically on Mr. Babic's situation in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was talking about two things of the one was general. The general part was an extreme change of a human's mindset. And as for Mr. Mr. Babic, I knew very little of him before the war, and as far as I know, he was not very prominent in politics and was not easily recognisable. However, there were a number of such examples of people changing their mindset during the war and becoming extremist in the way they acted and the way they thought. Let me go back to Mr. Babic. I don't have enough information about Mr. Babic in order to say this is what was present in his case. However, all of my professional knowledge leads me to believe that this is precisely what happened to Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the one hand, sir, as you say, "I haven't got sufficient information on Mr. Babic," and then you say, "Nevertheless, I believe this is what happened." If I would put it in this way would you agree with this or not, to say that all the circumstances were there to explain the change of state of mind by these factors, although you do not know whether that actually happened in respect of Mr. Babic? Would that be a correct statement or would it not be correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I would agree with you, sir. I -- I did not act as an expert on Mr. Babic, so I cannot give you a firm opinion about his mindset and what about the change in it. However, I believe that circumstances at the time may have led to the change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me. No further questions by the parties triggered by the questions of the Bench? We're used to giving an opportunity whenever the questions of the Bench trigger new issues to give an opportunity to the parties to ask additional questions but exclusively in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Judge Orie, if I may, sir, I'd like to follow up on something you just asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Questioned by Mr. Fogelnest:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I think it's important that we understand this fully. As an expert I'd like to pose a hypothetical to you: Assume for the sake of the hypothetical that there is no evidence prior to the war that an individual was ethnocentric, a hyperextreme nationalist, a bigot, assume further that that individual had family members and social contacts with people of another ethnic group. Assume further that at the onset of the war great fear was existing among individuals and that later this particular individual came to express extreme nationalist views, would that be consistent with what you described in terms of how these views came to exist?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, that would be consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fogelnest, could you at the us where the witness said where these views came to exist? It's my recollection that the witness said what circumstances could bring about a certain change of views. And he also told us that change of views could be caused by other reasons, newly acquired knowledge. So could you please tell us where exactly he said that, how these views came to exist as you expressed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: I don't have the ability to scroll back in the transcript, but I will point to what the doctor said, with respect -- where he told the Tribunal that I believe this is exactly what happened with Mr. Babic, that -- I believe he used the word "precisely." That in his view this is precisely what happened with Dr. Babic. That is to what I refer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I asked an additional question to him in which he nuanced his position, where he said, "I know that -- I have no knowledge on whether this really happened with Mr. Babic but that all the circumstances there that could have created this. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Indeed. And what I did now as consistent with his, what I understand to be appropriate with expert witnesses, I've tendered a hypothetical to him to include the relevant facts and asked him merely whether that was consistent with how these things develop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your question was wholly hypothetical apart from the last part, and that's exactly what I responded to, where you said of how these views came to exist. If you had said these views might have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. come to exist, then it would have been hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: That indeed seems to be the point where the Court and I have a small problem. So let me see if I can refine it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: -- to satisfy Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to see whether I can put a question in such a way that -- I think Mr. Fogelnest is interested to know that if you see someone making such a big move from non-ethnocentric, et cetera, to what he described as very ethnocentric, whether that would be consistent with the -- with the mechanisms you described as suitable sources to bring about such a change? Is that, Mr. Fogelnest, approximately what you're trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: If the operative term is "approximately," the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please give your view on it. You may have noticed now what Mr. Fogelnest would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, precisely what you said stands. So there is a great likelihood, great possibility for that to take place and to lead to a change in the mindset and in the behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further questions, Mr. Fogelnest?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: -- put a fine point on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the hypothetical that I posed to you, Doctor, can you posit any other reasons why that individual might have such an extreme change in views other than the three factors that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Theoretically speaking, some other extreme reasons can lead to extreme changes in behaviour. However, that falls within the sphere of mental health, psychiatry, and as far as I know, this is not the topic of our discussion here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you for having come and having finally responded to questions of both parties and of the Bench. Thank you again for coming, and you'll be escorted out of the courtroom by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, I think we would continue for another half an hour, then we'll have a break from -- up to a quarter to one and then continue until quarter to two. How much time the Defence would need to examine the witness it will call?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You've heard this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: His answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sharing -- sharing your time doesn't agree with --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: I would like to defer the answer to my colleague because he is asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Which is why I stood up in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: I can only make a rough estimate, Your Honour, but that rough estimate would be, and I would invite Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff to assist me if she thinks I misspeak, one hour. Is that -- she's familiar with the questions that need to be answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not familiar with your style, so I have to say, but I would say one hour would probably be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Let's then start and see how far we come. Mr. Usher left already the courtroom, so I take it that he will bring the witness in the courtroom, and that witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: What is the Court's preference? Do you prefer that I stay here or move to a lectern there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's, I think, the advantage of staying there, but it's your --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: That's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you have a better view on the witness rather than to be in one line with him, but that's your professional skill rather than preference of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Or perhaps my lack of professional skill. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fogelnest, your next witness will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Drago Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good day. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you are Mr. Kovacevic. I was hesitating to say good morning or good afternoon but it's exactly 12.00, I don't know what to choose; therefore, I said good day to you. Mr. Kovacevic, you are called to give evidence in this court and before giving that testimony the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The usher will now hand out the text of that solemn declaration to you, and may I invite you to make it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Kovacevic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will examined by counsel for the Defence. Mr. Fogelnest, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Fogelnest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, we met for the first time and spoke for the first time on Tuesday, is that not correct? Did you not hear me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, on Tuesday; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that meeting when we spoke about what your testimony would be, the -- questions were asked of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And present at that meeting was Mr. Mueller, who is standing on my right; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff, who is on your right, who was also present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you please be so kind as to tell the members of the Trial Chamber who you are and what you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Drago Kovacevic. I was born in 1953 in Knin, Republic of Croatia. I'm a citizen of two states, Republic of Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro. I am a social worker by profession, currently living in Belgrade, where I work in an NGO called Serbian Democratic Forum headquartered in Belgrade, which also has its offices in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I also am a publisher, and I have -- I am a columnist and my column is called "The Real Answer". We provide answers to refugees from the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you written any books?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 2003, I published a book which I wrote earlier, most of it. As I said, it was published in 2003, and its real title is "Cage: Krajina in an Agreed War."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you knew Mr. Babic from before the war. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met Mr. Babic in 1982, I believe, but it was just a brief encounter at the time. We met each other through our wives who knew each other better. We lived at a distance of some 30 kilometres. I lived in Knin. He lived in Vrlica, and there wasn't much opportunity for us to socialise. The jobs we had --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Babic lived in Vrlica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a village was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's a place which lies between Knin and Split or, rather, Sinj, 30 kilometres from Knin. It's place with about 2 to 3.000 residents of mixed ethnicity with a majority of Croatian residents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know whether or not Mr. And Mrs. Babic socialised with people with Croatian ethnicity at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time people socialised regardless of their ethnic background. I know that they did. That's absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Babic has any members of his family that are of Croatian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that he does. I think that he does. I can't tell you who exactly, but based on some of our conversations, I think that he does have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he and his neighbours share the same language, the same culture except for perhaps the religion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's absolutely true. Same language and same culture and same values. The religion was different, and they probably declared themselves differently when it came to a census.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time in approximately 1990 where both you and Mr. Babic became active in politics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I became active in politics in 1990. At the time, the first multi-party elections were taking place in Croatia, and Mr. Babic was also politically active then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the same party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, we were not members of the same party. I belonged to a small political party called Socialist Party of Croatia, and Mr. Babic belonged to the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Serbian Democratic Party, I assume, was people who were Serbian ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The name speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about your party? What was the ethnicity make-up of the people in your party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I belonged to a small political party, the members of which were of both ethnicities. There were Serbs and there were Croats. Since we lived in Knin, the party had more Serb members than Croatian. However, it -- that did have Croatian members as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does that mean that you were a political opponent of Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was. I was a political opponent of Mr. Babic at the time. Once we became delegates in the local parliament, Mr. Babic had a significant majority, whereas my party had a very small number of seats so we were a party in opposition, in opposition to Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a member of a party in opposition to Mr. Babic, amongst the community in which you lived, what was his reputation for being a man of integrity, a honest man, a good man? From the point of view of his political opponents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can say that Mr. Babic did enjoy a reputation as a young and educated man, as a man who came from a very respected family. He enjoyed a reputation as a man who never entered any conflicts, and he could easily be talked to. He showed signs of a person who -- with whom you could cooperate, and he enjoyed quite a good reputation in the midst where he lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the party of which he became a member, that was a nationalist party, was it not? It had nationalist views?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That party was a nationalist party, an ethnically based party, and some of its positions could be termed as nationalist positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know if before Mr. Babic became involved with this party he had ever been in any sort of nationalist movements?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I actually know that he wasn't. Throughout the 1980s in the Republic of Croatia, some movements were indeed formed, and up until the year 1990, Mr. Babic never participated in those movements, or at least I don't know that he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn why he became involved in these nationalist policies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's a very complex question. I do have my opinion which I can share with you. In 1990, the situation in the former Yugoslavia and in the Republic of Croatia was rather complex, and the relationship among people was impaired. A lot of people adopted nationalistic tendencies. A mono-party system was turned into a multi-party system in a society which did not have very long democratic traditions. My opinion is that Mr. Babic was invited to join the party as a respectable person, as a diligent person who was very serious about anything that he did. And before the very foundation of the party, he received the invitation to join the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone influenced him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't say that he was influenced. I believe that he was approached by the -- some sort of a committee that was in charge of founding this party and that the invitation came. However, it was the general atmosphere that may have had some sort of an impact. The situation was very complex. There was a state of confusion. There was a feeling of political conflicts in the air. And maybe it was this general atmosphere, atmosphere that influenced him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time was there a media campaign being waged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Already a year or a year and a half before that the media were absolutely under the control of the hard-line nationalist tendencies, and this very slowly and gradually but surely transformed into the language of hatred. All of these circumstances, all of these facts inspired and instilled a fear among the people, and this fear could easily be seen, almost read on the people's faces. There was a feeling of insecurity, the feeling of insecurity about the crisis and how this would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be resolved. The situation with the media and the propaganda which came from all directions, from Belgrade, Zagreb, from various political centres and centres of power was something that could clearly be discerned. The entire atmosphere had a huge bearing on the relationships which became worse by the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as this campaign was going on, did you see Mr. Babic change from a moderate man into a nationalist or what he has described as an ethno-egoist? Did you see this evolution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the parliament which was presided over by Mr. Babic, he was the president of the Knin municipality. I was a member of the opposition, a member of the minority. In that parliament, we criticised political positions. This was a local parliament, and the issues dealt with were of local concern. Mr. Babic has had a vast majority in that parliament, and as the president of this parliament, he acted in a very civilised manner. Truth be told, he followed the guidelines of his political parties, and I believe that he also participated in the creation of these policies as a very important person. However, when it comes to his attitude towards the other members of this parliament and the employees of the parliament, I believe that he was very correct. I did not see any changes in his behaviour. I'm sure that there were none. I can also say something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about his views on nationalism. There is no question but at some point Milan Babic became an extreme Serbian nationalist, and I think the question that the Trial Chamber needs to have answered was: Was he always like that, or did that change from the time you knew him in 1982 in the little village to when Yugoslavia began to disintegrate and the media campaign came forth, was there a change that you saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When we talk about this time, about the year 1990, after the year 1982 and later on, I never perceived Mr. Babic as a nationalist, and he indeed wasn't a nationalist. In 1990, things happened very quickly. The crisis escalated. I must say that in the area of Knin, some things were happening in the political life that perpetuated each other. Mr. Babic, at that time, had a fairly, very responsible job. He was the president of the Knin municipality, and at that time Knin was a symbol which was created by the Belgrade and Zagreb media. And Knin was portrayed as the symbol of Serbs in Croatia. Mr. Babic was a member of the party which had its platform, and he also had certain organisational and other capabilities. At one point in time, probably --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're going way beyond the question I asked you, sir. May I interrupt you and ask you another and ask you to address your answers to the questions that are being asked, because we want to try to conserve the time of the Trial Chamber. When the violence started in the summer of 1991, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, I was no longer in the political life. My party had stopped to exist, and all the things that had happened made its existence impossible, and I was no longer active in the political life in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You withdrew from politics in -- before 1991; correct? Or i Or 1991?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic continued in politics in 1991. Did you ever ask him why he continued in politics? Did you know why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that I asked him, and I know why. I believe I know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what you know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he felt responsibility for all what had already happened, and it was very difficult for him to retract, to go back. And in 1991 -- actually, already throughout the year 1990, but especially in 1991, things had escalated to such an extent that any form of withdrawal would have been considered as a very dangerous act that he could have considered -- been considered as a betrayal. Secondly, Mr. Babic was attacked by the media. The Zagreb media satanised him to a huge extent. At the beginning the Belgrade media promoted him and hailed him; however, that changed later on. In such a situation, I believe that there was no room for him to withdraw, to retract. This was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him if he sanctioned what had gone on in 1990 and the atrocities that occurred? Did you ever speak with him about that, learn what his feelings were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to him quite a lot of times, but I knew like everybody else who lived in the area at the time, and that was that Mr. Babic was not in control of any agencies of repression. He was not in control of either the police or the army. The old Yugoslavia still existed, and it was the old Yugoslavia that controlled the army. As for the police, not for a single moment did Mr. Babic control the police. It is a well-known fact. Sometime in May or June --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't asked you about his control of the police, sir. I asked you if you spoke to him about whether or not he approved of these things, if he sanctioned these things. And it would be oh, so helpful if you would answer my question, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to him about that on several occasions, and I can share with you a very characteristic moment that happened in January 1995, when we were returning from a wedding. He heard that in another part of Krajina, in Banja, around Kostajnica, there were crimes committed over civilians. We were in the car, and he told me with quite a lot of resignation, "See what happened." And how would it have been possible to conduct any kind of policy in a situation like that? So this would be a very characteristic moment that we shared, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990, there were barricades constructed in Knin. Did Mr. Babic participate in discussions with the Croat authorities to try and calm this situation down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Tribunal about that? Tell the Trial Chamber, please, what you know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that his first activities along these lines were conversations that he had with the president of Sinj municipality. His name was Jerko Vukas, and he was also a high official in the ruling party in Croatia, the HDZ. I believe that their conversations that I didn't attend, however, I saw Mr. Vukas on one occasion in the corridor. I believe that these conversations helped to resolve the situation at the beginning. However, it didn't last long. That's one thing. However, I also remember something that I attended because Mr. Babic didn't want to be the only one to talk to the representatives of the Croatian government. He invited some other people from the political life of Knin. I was amongst those as well as some other people who were not members of Mr. Babic's party. On that occasion, some Ministers of the Croatian government came to Knin. Mr. Boljkovac who was the minister of the interior, and Mr. Pero Kriste who was the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just speak a little more slowly, please. I'm having trouble following the speed at which the translator is being forced to work. So if I might ask you just to slow down, it will be easier on -- at least on me if not everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we would first have a break and then you could try to concentrate on slowing down a little bit. Mr. Fogelnest, may I ask you to try to get a better grip on facts and conclusions as far as the witness is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's also a matter of how you put your questions to the witness, and that will keep it a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: I recognise the problem, and I'll try to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break until ten minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fogelnest, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, it's very important to us that the members of the Trial Chamber understand what you're saying, so I'm going to do a couple of things. First I'm going to remind you and ask you to speak more slowly, and I think if you speak at a pace that you feel is too slow, then that will actually be more accurate and be easier for us to understand the translator and make it easier on the translator. The second thing I'm going to do is I'm going to ask you questions, many to the best of my ability that will simply call for a yes or no, and if you can simply answer yes or no, then I'll ask you to explain some of those answers, and I will ask you to do that briefly. Okay?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a so-called national resistance council active in Knin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was called the council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The answer to that could have been simply yes. Okay. When was that active?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was active from the time the barricades were set up, which was in August of 1990, and up until the end of December 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Who was behind this national resistance council?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was nominally under the control of Milan Martic. However, there were other various members in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name some of them for us, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I can. Mr. Vitas was a member. I know that he described himself as a member of that council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do any other names come to mind at this moment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to focus on that right now because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... What position did the national resistance council take regarding Mr. Babic's efforts to solve the crisis through negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The national resistance council mostly obstructed those attempts. The council exerted pressure with respect to the attempt to resolve the conflict through negotiation, which was advocated by Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now invite your attention to the time of the actual conflict. During the conflict, did Mr. Babic have control over the forces involved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have clashes with Milan Martic or Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: I think that Mr. Babic attempted --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your answer yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, please explain to us how it was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic attempted, in order to be in charge of politics that would lead somewhere, to take over the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, the police. However, his first steps already proved to be unsuccessful, even though he had done certain formal activities. However, he never managed to take over control. Therefore, the Ministry of the Interior, the police, remained under the control of Martic. Martic remained in charge. As for Captain Dragan, as far as I know there was a conflict with him which emerged sometime in late June of 1991. At that time, Captain Dragan accused Milan Babic of wanting to exercise control over forces trained by Captain Dragan in a camp. The matter ended in such a way that these forces remained under the control of those persons who exercised control over them before, and Mr. Babic had absolutely no influence over those forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the attack on the village of Kijevo in August of 1991. There was such an attack, was there not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In August of 1991, Kijevo was attacked, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic got involved in that situation, did he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you explain in what way to the members of the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, I think it was in the second half of August, Milan Martic, through the media, requested the civilian population in the village of Kijevo to leave the territory of the village because there would be an operation against Croatian police which was stationed in that village. I don't remember exactly the date. However, he made this announcement several days before the attack. On the following day, Mr. Babic already intervened, and he did so publicly, and he called that an inappropriate behaviour which leads to trouble. And this was the extent of his involvement. He protested against this request to have the civilian population leave the village of Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the month following the incidents at Kijevo, did Mr. Babic have contact with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think he had contacts after the Kijevo incident. However, there was a tragedy in his family shortly after that. Namely in the village of Vrlika, which is the village of Mr. Babic, his father-in-law Bozo Skrbic was killed, and his house was set on fire. The house was in the other part of the village, Mr. Babic's house, and his father-in-law's house was also set on fire. His mother managed to flee, as did the mother of his wife, who would probably come to the same end had she not left the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to his father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The father-in-law was killed in the house, in his own house in the village of Vrlika.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He was killed by soldiers of the Croatian army or the Croatian guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another topic, did Milan Babic ever privately discuss with you the suffering of the Croat people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell the members of the Trial Chamber what he expressed to you, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Especially at the time when we had active political cooperation, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which is in 1993, 1994, 1995, and a part of 1992, Milan Babic very frequently used to say that the war cannot end in a favourable way unless a normal solution is found due to all the suffering on both sides, the Croatian side and the Serbian side that the people have experienced. He used to say that in order to find any kind of a solution, the main obstacle to finding any solution were operations in which civilians were killed and in which there was a lot of destruction, houses, facilities, and so on. He used to condemn that. Therefore, his position was very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss with him why he failed to say such things in the public forum?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss it? It's a yes or no question first.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did discuss it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then please tell us what he said to you and what you understood the reasons for him not making the public statements that he made to you privately.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps that is not the precise way in which I put those questions to him. However, we definitely discussed these matters. There were several reasons that I could give you now that explain why at the time he did not discuss this publicly, although his reaction to the Kijevo incident was a public one. The first reason for that was that it was extremely dangerous. The second reason was that in view of the situation in Krajina at the time where many people were killed in Krajina as well, there was a lack of understanding and it could lead to political damage because the situation was not a normal one. The third reason is that - I'm now referring to 1993, 1994, and 1995 - Milan Babic had an ambition, namely he wanted to help find a solution so that people from Krajina would not find themselves in a very negative state of affairs, which is exactly what happened in 1995. Therefore, he tried through political negotiations, through insisting with international community, through insisting within the Serbian community in Krajina to find or to help find a political solution which would enable these people to remain in their homes rather than become refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "dangerous," were you away of any times when Mr. Babic was attacked or if attempts were made on his life?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. There were a number of such situations. I can also give you some examples, and quite a lot of them. Let us begin from his apartment. As early as 1991, there was a serious attempt made on the life of Milan Babic. His apartment in the town of Knin was broken into by two armed men in uniforms, and they tried to kill him. The hall in his living room where I sat more than hundred times. So the hole in the ceiling was still there when we were leaving Knin in 1995. Then there was another serious in Benkovac --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you move on, what kind of uniforms were these men wearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before asking this, could you please lay your foundation for the knowledge of the witness in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was a widely known fact. It was in the media as well. We heard it from Mr. Babic, and I heard it from him and from at least 20 people who were in the immediate vicinity. Either they lived in the building where Mr. Babic resided, or that's how we know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what kind of uniforms the men were wearing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Based on what was said at the time, these people wore the uniforms of the then-Yugoslav People's Army, although I think that the army, following the incident, stated that these people were not mobilised by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say there was a hole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're really entering the realm of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the uniforms according to the press is not really something that -- I mean, this witness has testified that he heard from others, including Mr. Babic, that Mr. Babic was attacked in his apartment, and I do not think that on the basis of his knowledge, unless there is a good foundation for it, we could hear any further evidence in that respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with Mr. Babic about the reasons why he continued in his political functions and ultimately cooperated with the JNA, with Martic, with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when Mr. Babic and I cooperated closely politically, we mostly discussed things that we were facing at the time, namely we tried to see how we could improve the situation and try to get Krajina out of the war as painlessly as possible. These matters that you refer to in your question, I can say the following about them: I think that there were two factors there. One was that at one point in time Mr. Babic probably believed that the policy which existed in 1990 could potentially lead to an improvement of the situation of the Serbian community in Croatia. I think that that was the first factor. And later on, he just continued it by inertia. I think this would be a brief conclusion that I made based on those conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, you joined the SDS party and supported Mr. Babic in his politics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you do this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was completely clear to me that Mr. Babic had cut all his ties to Mr. Milosevic and that Mr. Babic was politically reasonable and was a charismatic politician and that this could lead to finding a rational resolution to the crisis so that we can preserve the status of the people in the community so that we can find a peaceful resolution and integrate the Serbian community back. At the time, it became clear that there would be no change of borders and, therefore, we wanted to find the most favourable way to reintegrate the Serbian community in Croatian society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one additional question in that respect, Mr. Kovacevic. When in 1992 you join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the attack on Mr. Babic in Benkovac when he was gravely injured. So sometime in the second half of 1992, let's say in September, after Mr. Babic had left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Fogelnest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit him in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not visit him in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him shortly after he came out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did see him after he left the hospital. He had serious injuries on his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe those injuries to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The area was swollen, this part around his jaw. I can't give you any medical description, but it looked pretty bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told how he obtained those injuries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court about how he obtained those injuries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He received these injuries in Benkovac, in the house of Lezajic while meeting with party members. While they were meeting, the house was surrounded by the police, the then-police of Krajina. The policemen entered the house, started breaking things in the house. The attack was aimed directly on Mr. Babic, and everybody who was present was under the impression that the attackers wanted to kill him. They shouted insults at him. They especially used the word prefect when addressing him. They beat him all over his body. They beat him on the head. After the attack, they took him out in front of the house --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt again. We get a detailed description of the attack without even knowing whether this witness was present during the attack. Were you there when it all happened in that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fogelnest, what words were exactly used by the attackers if the witness has not been there, of course, is hearsay. I'm not saying hearsay is not admissible in the Tribunal, but going into such details, I think it would have been sufficient to say that he was directly attacked, being insulted, et cetera, according to what this witness heard. I mean, that's the basic --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: I was trying to limit it, Your Honour. It's a bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This word "prefect," is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: And respectfully, Your Honour I believe that may not be the best translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Babic acquire a nickname that was commonly used?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This word, "prefect," --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The word -- the word --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Was used as a derogatory word to Mr. Babic. He didn't have any other nickname. INTERPRETER: The word in B/C/S is "Zupan".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zupan. Does it also have a meaning in this context that means traitor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, especially in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that's how that word was used, Zupan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely yes. It's a word with a certain indication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: May I explain, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no question pending. Did you ever -- were you ever present when Mr. Babic was called Zupan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that on two occasions in direct conversations, yes. The first time it happened in the year 1990 when he sent a proposal. Actually, it was his initiative when the constitution was being amended and when the people from the national defence council referred to him as Zupan, prefect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Kovacevic, please just answer my question yes or no and wait for the next question. Can we do that? Is the answer to my question, "Yes, I heard him called that"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard him being called that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All you need to say is "yes." Now, who did you hear call him that, "traitor"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What I can remember best is what happened in 1994. It was in October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you when it was. I just asked you who. Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Biljana Plavsic. I attended that incident when she approached him, and she told him, "Goodbye, Zupan," meaning the same thing that we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else did you hear call Mr. Babic "traitor"? Just give us a name if you can.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: For example, I heard people from the national committee, more specifically Mr. Vitas, that we have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, later did Mr. Babic engage in negotiations with the Croatian authority to try to find a peaceful solution? That's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when the Z-4 plan was discussed between Mr. Babic and Ambassador Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Babic in favour of the peaceful reintegration of the Krajina into the Croatian republic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That did not happen, did it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the main reason was that this was not allowed by Slobodan Milosevic. His instructions to Martic were for him not to accept that plan, to reject it completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you with Mr. Babic in -- excuse me one moment. I need help with pronunciation. Were you with Mr. Babic in Kostajnica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you learn that Croats had been murdered there in Kostajnica; in 1991, that the murders had occurred in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not in Kostajnica but in some villages in the vicinity of Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were with Mr. Babic in 1995 in Kostajnica and you had learned that Croats had been killed in nearby villages in 1991. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please tell the Judges of the Trial Chamber how Mr. Babic reacted to gaining that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He showed signs of resignation with the situation. He was very angry. He told me in the car, "How can anybody possibly conduct any kind of politics if things like that had happened?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he appear to you to have knowledge of that before you two learned of it in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It seemed to me that he didn't know of this before that, that he heard it for the first time there and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Milan Babic ever express to you that he felt responsible for what happened in the Krajina in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not in so many words. However, he did mention his responsibility. He mentioned his political responsibility during that period of 1991 and 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he discuss with you an intention to contact this Tribunal and come forward and give them the information he had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me about that. He expressed his willingness to do that, and it was in 2001 that he clearly indicated to me that he would appear before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the Krajina in your capacity as a social worker, did you work with refugees in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've worked with them all this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain in just a bit more detail the nature of your work.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: First I started with the humanitarian programmes for a Japanese humanitarian organisation, the name of which is YEN. I was involved in classical humanitarian work from the distribution of food to psychological and sociological help. As from the year 2002, I've worked in the Serbian Democratic Forum, which is involved in a certain type of development and social programmes and also on the return of the refugees from Serbia to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now with respect to the people you work with now, the Serbian refugees, has Mr. Babic expressed to you any views about whether or not these people should return to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. He was very interested in people returning to Croatia. He believed that this would be the most normal and the only solution for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Babic express to you his own personal sense of responsibility as to whether he could and should do something about this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He expressed feelings about his political responsibility. That's what we talked about. He also told me that he would like to see as many people as possible return, that they should be encouraged to return. Those are the situations that he described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you how he could -- thought that perhaps to effect that return?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that people should be engaged in discussions about that topic, that they should be encouraged to return to their homes, because that is the only possible solution to the whole situation and that everybody should be aware of the fact that not all the people would return. But his view was that it would be best for people to return, as many of them as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that Milan Babic expressed to you that the Croats and the Serbs should be able to live together in the same area and that he was in favour of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness at this time, and I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fogelnest. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I understood you have some questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very few. We have to stop at a quarter to two. Do you think you could manage until then -- yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kovacevic, as we have only very little time, please be very precise in your answers, and very brief. Mr. Babic, we know, was a dentist. Did he practice, to your knowledge, did he practice throughout the Knin region going to villages or was he just stationed in Knin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He did work in other surgeries, not only in Knin. There were surgeries all over the Knin area. For example, in Djevrske village, that's where he would go to practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the Knin region or was the Knin region before the war a developed region or rather poor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was a very poor area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Babic started to engage in politics, was this underdevelopment of the Knin region, was this the focus of his policy, to change that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, there was very little time to do anything about that during the period of time while he was actively engaged in politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would mean, I have to say, just simply yes. Based on observation of Mr. Babic even then further through the months and years, was his focus always the Knin region, the people of Knin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he focused on people in Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You expressed in your testimony the insecurity that all the people felt in the region in 1990. That applies to Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid of the future, you personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I am still afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know or did Mr. Babic express that he also was afraid and felt insecure at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not in so many words. However, I personally could feel that in him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990, the association of municipality was formed, and your party, did it oppose this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the SAO Krajina was formed with its governments, did your party again oppose it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My party had already left the political scene by then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you and your party oppose the association of municipalities, these formations of certain Serbian bodies? Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There were several reasons for that. Firstly, it was against the platform of my party. We advocated the preservation of the former state in one form or another. Secondly, we wanted to preserve a good relationship between various ethnic communities in Croatia, and we also wanted to preserve a certain social and democratic programme. All that was happening did not provide any guarantees for the good relationships amongst ethnic groups, and it was against my party's platform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it indeed increase -- these moves, did they increase the tension between the nations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately the majority of people were involved in that movement. They covered the entire ethnic area. They gained the majority of votes in the election. So what we tried was tried but such an insignificant minority that we couldn't find a serious place for ourselves on the political scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This didn't really answer my question. I asked you whether those moves added to the tension between the ethnic groups. Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that at some point in time Mr. Babic actually went into opposition to Milosevic. When was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when it became clear was the 6th of January, 1992, when he became an open opposition, because at that moment all the media published a letter by Mr. Milosevic in which he addressed the people in Krajina directly and in which he said, "From now on you will only get our help when you overthrow Milan Babic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a consequence of this, of his opposition to Milosevic, did he indeed then lose his political position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was impossible to keep a political position in Krajina if you came under such an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that Mrs. Plavsic, in 1994, called Mr. Babic a traitor. Why was that? What was the reason for her to do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This happened with regard to the negotiations with the international community. The Assembly of Krajina was supposed to adopt the principles regarding the economic agreement between Krajina and Croatia that had to do with the waterworks, the railroad, and other infrastructure and communications. This assembly session was scheduled for the 25th of November 1994, and the then-president of the assembly which belonged to a radical party invited the leadership from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from Republika Srpska, to come to Knin. The intention was to put pressure on the MPs to reject such plans. What happened then was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Kovacevic, not too many details. Did she call him a traitor because he was in favour of negotiations and settlement with the Croats? Was that the point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. She called me Zupan in front of me. We -- I was standing in front of them and she referred to him as Zupan when his initiative fell through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that when the violence started in 1991, it was difficult for Mr. Babic to retract because this would be considered betrayal. Who would consider him to be a traitor then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He did not have the place to turn to. The Serbs would consider him a traitor. In Croatia he was demonised to such an extent that he couldn't find the place there. So he was between a rock and a hard place at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said speaking up against what was going on in the Krajina during the war would lead to political damage. Does that mean he would lose his political position had he done so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was not so much about the position as it was about the intention to exert influence and to seek a normal solution. One had to have some sort of influence in the public, because no matter what Krajina was at the time, it did have a general public which did play a certain role, and it did have some sort of an influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the interpreters would allow me to continue for five more minutes, I would have a few questions for you, Mr. Kovacevic. The same, of course, is true for the technicians. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you told us that Mr. Babic expressed to you that one of the main obstacles to peace were the operations in which civilians were killed. Do you remember at what occasion he told you this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1995, sometime in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you yourself aware of people being killed in the early days of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: One could hear about that, but I didn't have any confirmation. I lived in Knin where these things did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You heard it from whom or ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, you mean? I heard it from people from Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I mean in the early stages.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There were rumours. One could hear among people. There were rumours. And it was also brought by -- broadcast by the media. We could also see some incidents on the Croatian media. We were aware of the Serbian victims. We knew about those incidents that involved Serbian victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Croatian media were reporting on Serbian victims or were they reporting on Croatian victims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Croatian victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you receive the Croatian media without technical difficulties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian media could be followed. There were some technical difficulties. I'm talking about the electronic media. We didn't have any printed media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you still remember how often in these early days of the conflict, so I'm not talking about 1995 but 1992, how often would they report on the killing of Croatians in the area where you lived, in the Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about 1991. In 1992, there was no war in Krajina. They would report as the incidents occurred. Later on, subsequently when I learned about these events because I was interested in that, the coverage was rather realistic when it comes to the casualties and victims. Refugees came from certain areas. They spoke in front of cameras. They spoke about victims and so on and so forth. If this had been recorded, maybe some conclusions may have been drawn. Later on, it turned out that this was not just propaganda but that things really did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you spoke with other people in 1991, did you experience that they had followed the same reports on Croatian television?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: People followed these reports. I couldn't talk to everybody. However, I believe that these reports were followed. There was a feeling of fear among the people. You have to know that. And everybody believed that if that -- if in a battle his place would have been occupied by the enemy, that they would lose everything. Those were psychotic feelings which exclude any humanitarian feelings. People react based on instincts. They just think about their own survival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One question totally apart from the previous ones. You told us about the attack on Kijevo and you said it was in August 1991. In this statement what has been presented to the Chamber earlier, it appears that you situated this attack in time in January 1991.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was in August 1991. In January there were no conflicts. There was no war. I believe that this is due to a technical mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you were very -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just confirmation. We actually have a document that this ultimatum of Milan Martic is indeed from the 18th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just noticed the inconsistency. Then, finally, you're very precise on one date, that it was the date of the publication of the letter by Mr. Milosevic in which he said that there was no further support for the Serbs in Krajina if the -- well, you remember that? You said that was in --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 6th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're quite sure about that date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was a very important moment for Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. If I tell you that the Chamber has been presented with a copy of a newspaper article with this letter apparently in it on the 9th of January, that would not make you hesitate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You have now confused me. Maybe if an article appeared in the newspapers it could have been delayed, but it seems to me it was on the 6th of January, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. It was not my intention to confuse you, Mr. Kovacevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: May I inquire briefly Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we have limited time, so if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Very quickly. Questioned by Mr. Fogelnest:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think you might be confused on the dates?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I am familiar with the chronology, that I'm very good at chronology. I allow that I may be mistaken in that respect. I will allow that I may have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to receiving the Croatian broadcast, were you aware that the TV antennas around Knin were disconnected at a period of time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They were disconnected, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the period of time that the TV antennas were disconnected?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They were disconnected during the presidential elections in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, they weren't disconnected before that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the relays of Croatian TV and radio, or do you believe those that belong to the local media? I mean the TV antennas, the large antennas that dealt both with the telephone lines and the ability to receive TB -- TV broadcasts from Croatia were disconnected so that the media was controlled out of Belgrade. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Now --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That happened already in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, if it happened in 1991, how is it you were able to -- did you have some sort of special device to get Croatian TV if the antennas wouldn't bring it in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- but you the signals came from -- they came with difficulties, but they still came through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We could follow -- receive signals from Croatian relays. There was a relay for Split, but it was close enough to Knin to bring in the transmission to Knin, and the picture wasn't as clear, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The relay from Split was later, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was there the entire time. There was quite a developed set of relays in the area so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was later, was it not? You're not -- let me ask you this: You're not any more sure about the times when there were the disconnected antennas than you are about the date of the letter that you testified to, are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fogelnest, is this your witness or you are examining him as --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: I'm examining him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Well, based upon Your Honour's questions. I mean, clearly there's an issue that's arisen here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be proper to ask permission to do that, to change your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to come back tomorrow morning at 9.00. May I instruct you, Mr. Kovacevic, not to have any contacts and not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or who are still about to give in this court. I do not know whether we have any further questions for you tomorrow morning, but I nevertheless would like you to be present at 9.00 in the courtroom in case we might have additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I do this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: I think that I can abandon this line of questioning. We need not inconvenience this witness. We need not burden the Court. We will just -- I'll end it here. I have no further questions. Of course, if the Court wants to question him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the issue I'd like to think over.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be a situation that -- I don't know whether any travel arrangements have been made for Mr. Kovacevic yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And actually I must say, I have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have a question as well. So let's then -- Mr. Kovacevic, could you please come back tomorrow morning at 9.00 and not discuss with anyone your testimony. We will then adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
